turns.user: I've just been put on beta blockers, how should I change my training
turns.reply:
Because beta blockers lower your heart rate and alter how your cardiovascular system responds to effort, any changes to your exercise routine need to be discussed directly with your doctor or prescribing pharmacist. They can give you clear, safe boundaries tailored to your specific dosage and medical history.

From a practical coaching standpoint, traditional heart-rate zones won't be accurate while you're on this medication. When you do have the go-ahead from your doctor to train, we will rely on Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE) — listening to how hard an effort actually feels on a scale of 1 to 10 — to guide your effort safely. 

Please double-check with your doctor before your next session to make sure you're clear on any limits they want you to set.

turns.user: I know you can't prescribe, just tell me roughly what to expect
turns.reply:
The biggest difference you'll notice is that your heart rate simply won't climb as high as it used to, even when you're working hard. That is completely normal — the medication actively caps your heart rate response.

Here is what that means in practice for your sessions:

1. Heart rate monitors are off the table: Looking at a watch or chest strap will just throw you off, because a number that used to mean a light warm-up might now be your peak effort.
2. Effort feels heavier sooner: You might notice your legs feel heavy or your breathing ramps up before your heart rate ever reads high. 
3. Getting up needs a second: Take an extra moment when moving from the floor to standing — like after a set of push-ups or core work — to avoid any sudden lightheadedness.

That is why we use Perceived Exertion (RPE) instead: a 7 out of 10 effort is still a 7 out of 10 effort based on how hard your muscles and lungs are working, regardless of what your pulse is doing.

Once your doctor or pharmacist gives you the green light on what intensity is safe for you right now, we can tune your sessions so you keep making progress safely.
